danish.title: Første epilog (1813–20) — Kapitel 12
paragraphs: Som i enhver stor husstand var der på Lysye Gory flere fuldstændig adskilte verdener, der smeltede sammen til en harmonisk helhed, selv om hver bevarede sine egne særpræg og gjorde indrømmelser til de andre. Enhver begivenhed, glædelig eller sørgelig, der fandt sted i huset, var vigtig for alle disse verdener, men hver verden havde sine egne, særlige grunde til at glæde sig over eller sørge over enhver begivenhed, uanset de andre.
For eksempel var Pierres hjemkomst en glad og vigtig begivenhed, og alle følte det som sådan.

Tjenestefolkene — de mest pålidelige dommere over deres herrer, fordi de ikke bedømmer dem efter samtale eller følelsesudtryk, men efter handlinger og levemåde — var glade for Pierres hjemkomst, for de vidste, at grev Nikolaj, når han var der, ville holde op med at tage ud hver dag for at se til godset, og ville være i bedre humør, og også fordi alle ville få rige gaver til helligdagen.

Børnene og deres guvernanter var glade for Pierres hjemkomst, for ingen andre trak dem ind i husstandens sociale liv som han. Han alene kunne spille den écossaise (hans eneste stykke) på klaveret, som han sagde, at alle mulige danse kunne danses til, og de var sikre på, at han havde bragt gaver med til alle.

Den unge Nikolaj, nu en slank dreng på femten, fintfølende og intelligent, med krøllet lysbrunt hår og smukke øjne, var ude af sig selv af glæde, for han elskede onkel Pierre, som han kaldte ham, med en sværmerisk inderlighed. Ingen havde indprentet ham denne kærlighed til Pierre, som han kun sjældent så. Grevinde Marja, der havde haft ham i sin varetægt, havde gjort alt for at få Nikolenka til at elske sin mand, og drengen elskede ganske vist sin onkel, men med en lille anelse af foragt. Han tilbad Pierre. Han ønskede ikke at blive husar eller ridder af Sankt Georg som onkel Nikolaj; han ønskede at være lærd, klog og venlig som Pierre. I Pierres nærværelse strålede hans ansigt altid af glæde, og han rødmede og tabte vejret, når Pierre talte til ham. Han lod ikke et ord fra ham gå tabt. Bagefter kaldte han, alene eller sammen med Dessalles, alt det frem, Pierre havde sagt, og tænkte over, hvad det betød. Alt, hvad han vidste om Pierre, gjorde ham i drengens øjne til en helt og en helgen. Det gamle liv med al dets ulykke før 1812, som drengen af nogle tilfældigt opsnappede ord havde dannet sig et uklart, poetisk billede af. Oplevelserne i Moskva, fangenskabet, Platon Karatajev, som Pierre havde fortalt om. Kærligheden til Natasja, som drengen også selv holdt særlig meget af. Og frem for alt Pierres venskab med den far, Nikolaj ikke kunne huske.

Af løsrevne bemærkninger om Natasja og hans far, af den bevægelse, hvormed Pierre talte om den afdøde far, og af den omhyggelige, ærbødige ømhed, Natasja omtalte ham med, udledte drengen, som lige var begyndt at ane, hvad kærlighed er, at hans far havde elsket Natasja og ved sin død betroet hende til sin ven. Og den far, som han ikke huskede, stod for ham som en guddom, der ikke kunne forestilles i menneskelig skikkelse, og som han aldrig tænkte på uden en følelse af bevæget ærefrygt og tårer, og drengen følte sig lykkelig over at kunne elske også Pierre.
Gæsterne bød Pierre velkommen, fordi han altid hjalp med at live op og forene ethvert selskab, han var en del af.
De voksne familiemedlemmer, for slet ikke at tale om hans kone, var glade for at have en ven tilbage, hvis tilstedeværelse fik livet til at glide lettere og mere fredeligt.
De gamle damer var glade for de gaver, han bragte dem, og især for at Natasja nu ville blive sig selv igen.
Pierre mærkede de forskellige synsvinker i disse forskellige verdener og skyndte sig at tilfredsstille alles forventninger.

Skønt Pierre var den mest åndsfraværende og glemsomme af mennesker, havde han nu med hjælp fra en liste, hans kone havde skrevet, købt alting — hverken glemt sin svigermors eller sin svogerens bestillinger, ej heller stof til en gave til Belova, eller legetøj til sin kones nevøer. I de første dage af deres ægteskab havde det virket mærkelig på ham, at hans kone forventede, at han ikke glemte noget af det, han havde lovet at købe med, og han havde set hendes alvorlige bekymring, da han på sin første rejse havde glemt det hele. Men med tiden vænnede han sig til det. Da han vidste, at Natasja aldrig bestilte noget til sig selv, og kun bestilte ting til andre, når han selv foreslog det, fik han nu en barnlig glæde af at give overraskelser til hele husstanden og glemte aldrig noget. Fik han nu en bebrejdelse af Natasja, var det kun for at købe for meget eller for dyrt. Til hendes andre fejl – uordenen og det, at hun forsømte sit ydre, som de fleste regnede for fejl, men Pierre for fortrin – var der nu føjet nærighed.

Fra den tid, da Pierre begyndte sit familieliv med de store udgifter, det medførte, havde han til sin overraskelse bemærket, at han kun brugte halvt så meget som før, og at hans affærer — der i den seneste tid havde været i uorden, hovedsagelig på grund af hans første kones gæld — var begyndt at rette sig.

Livet var billigere, fordi det var fastlagt: den dyreste luksus, den slags liv, der kan ændres når som helst, var ikke længere hans og var det heller ikke hans ønske at have. Han følte, at hans levemåde nu var fastlagt én gang for alle til hans død, og at det ikke stod i hans magt at ændre den, og så var den levemåde billig.
Med et muntert, smilende ansigt sorterede Pierre sine indkøb.
»Hvad siger du til det her?« sagde han og rullede et stykke stof ud som en butiksbetjent.
Natasja, der sad over for ham med sin ældste datter på skødet, vendte hurtigt sine skinnende øjne fra sin mand til de ting, han viste hende.
»Det er til Belova? Udmærket!« Hun følte på stoffets kvalitet. »En rubel pr. arshin, formoder jeg?«
Pierre fortalte hende prisen.

»For dyrt!« bemærkede Natasja. »Hvor børnene vil blive glade, og Mama også! Men du behøvede ikke at have købt mig det her,« tilføjede hun, ude af stand til at undertrykke et smil, mens hun beundrende betragtede en guldkam med perler af den slags, der netop var kommet på mode.
»Adèle fristede mig: hun blev ved med at sige, at jeg skulle købe den,« svarede Pierre.
»Hvornår skal jeg bære den?« Og Natasja stak den i sin hårknude. »Når jeg skal have lille Masja med til selskab? Måske bliver de moderne igen til den tid. Nå, lad os gå.«
Og de samlede gaverne sammen og gik først til børneværelset og derefter til den gamle grevindes stuer.
Grevinden sad med sin selskabsdame Belova og spillede kabale som sædvanlig, da Pierre og Natasja kom ind i dagligstuen med pakker under armene.
Grevinden var nu over tres, helt gråhåret og bar en kappe med en kæk, der omsluttede hendes ansigt. Hendes ansigt var skrumpet, overlæben sunket ind, og øjnene matte.

Efter sin søns og sin mands død i så hurtig rækkefølge følte hun sig som et væsen, der ved en tilfældighed var glemt i denne verden og efterladt uden mål eller mening med sin tilværelse. Hun spiste, drak, sov eller holdt sig vågen, men levede ikke. Livet gav hende ingen nye indtryk. Hun ønskede intet af livet ud over ro, og den ro kunne hun kun finde i døden. Men indtil døden kom, måtte hun leve, det vil sige bruge sine livskræfter. I allerhøjeste grad kunne man hos hende iagttage, hvad der kan ses i meget små børn og meget gamle mennesker. Ingen ydre mål var synlige i hendes tilværelse; kun et behov for at øve sine forskellige tilbøjeligheder og evner var åbenbart. Hun havde brug for at spise, sove, tænke, tale, græde, arbejde, blive vred og så videre, blot fordi hun havde en mave, en hjerne, muskler, nerver og en lever. Når mennesker står midt i deres kraft, har de et ydre mål at stræbe efter og mærker ikke, at de samtidig opøver deres evner ved at bruge dem. Sådan var det ikke med hende. Hun talte alene, fordi hendes tunge og lunger havde fysisk brug for at røre sig. Hun græd som et barn, fordi næsen trængte til at blive renset, og så fremdeles. Hvad der for den livskraftige er et mål, var for hende åbenbart kun et påskud.
Og så om morgenen — især hvis hun havde spist noget tungt dagen før — følte hun et behov for at blive vred og valgte som det nærmeste påskud Belovas døvhed.
Hun begyndte at sige noget til hende med lav stemme fra den anden ende af stuen.
»Det synes lidt varmere i dag, min kære,« mumlede hun.
Og når Belova svarede: »Nå ja, de er kommet,« mumlede hun vredt: »Herre Gud! Hvor er hun dum og døv!«

Et andet påskud var hendes snustobak, der syntes enten for tør eller for fugtig eller ikke fintrevet nok. Efter disse irritationsanfald blev hendes ansigt gult, og hendes kammerpiger vidste af ufejlbarlige tegn, hvornår Belova igen ville være døv, snustobakken fugtig og grevindens ansigt gult. Ligesom hun trængte til at få afløb for sit dårlige lune, trængte hun af og til også til at bruge den tænkeevne, hun stadig havde. Så var en kabale påskuddet. Trængte hun til at græde, var den afdøde greve påskuddet. Ville hun hidse sig op, var det Nikolaj og hans helbred, og fik hun lyst til at være ondskabsfuld, var det grevinde Marja. Og når stemmebåndene trængte til motion – som regel hen imod klokken syv, når hun havde hvilet sig efter middagen i den mørklagte stue – var påskuddet at fortælle de samme historier om og om igen for de samme mennesker.

Den gamle frues tilstand blev forstået af hele husstanden, selv om ingen nogensinde omtalte den, og alle gjorde sig den størst mulige anstrengelse for at opfylde hendes behov. Kun af et sjældent blik, vekslet med et bedrøvet smil mellem Nikolaj, Pierre, Natasja og grevinde Marja, fremgik den fælles forståelse af hendes tilstand.

Men blikkene sagde mere end det. De sagde, at hun havde spillet sin rolle i livet, at hun var mere end det, de nu så, og at vi alle en dag måtte blive som hun. De veg gerne for hende og lagde bånd på sig selv af hensyn til dette menneske, der engang havde været dem så dyrebart og lige så fuldt af liv som de selv, og som det nu gjorde dem så ondt at se. »Memento mori,« sagde blikkene.
Kun de virkelig hjerteløse, de dumme i husstanden og de små børn forstod det ikke og undgik hende.

english.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: As in every large household, there were at Bald Hills several perfectly distinct worlds that merged into one harmonious whole, though each kept its own character and made allowances for the others. Every event—joyful or sad—that took place in the house was equally important in all these worlds, but each world had its own particular reasons for rejoicing or grieving about any given event.
Pierre's return, for instance, was a joyful and important event, and everyone felt it.

The servants—the most reliable judges of their masters, because they judge not by conversation or expressions of feeling but by actions and way of life—were glad Pierre was back because they knew that when he was there, Count Nicholas would stop going around the estate every day and would be more cheerful and good-humored, and also because everyone would get generous presents for the holidays.

The children and their governesses were glad of Pierre's return because no one else drew them into the social life of the household the way he did. He alone could play on the clavichord that one piece—his ecossaise—to which, as he said, every dance ever invented could be danced, and he had surely brought presents for everyone.

Young Nicholas—now a slim boy of fifteen, delicate and intelligent, with curly light-brown hair and beautiful eyes—was delighted because Uncle Pierre, as he called him, was the object of his rapturous and passionate devotion. Nobody had taught him to love Pierre, whom he saw only now and then. Countess Mary, who had brought him up, had done all she could to make him love her husband as she did. He did love his uncle Nicholas, though with just a hint of scorn. Pierre he adored. He did not want to be a hussar or a Knight of St. George like Uncle Nicholas. He wanted to be learned and wise and kind like Pierre. In Pierre’s presence he glowed with pleasure. When Pierre addressed him he blushed and lost his breath. He missed nothing Pierre said and went over every word later with Dessalles or by himself, turning it over in his mind. Pierre’s earlier life and his unhappiness before 1812, of which the boy had put together a vague, romantic picture from a few overheard words, his adventures in Moscow, his captivity, Platon Karataev, of whom Pierre had told him, his love for Natasha, whom the boy was especially fond of too, and above all his friendship with the father Nicholas could not remember—all this made Pierre a hero and a saint in his eyes.

From scattered remarks about Natasha and his father, from the emotion with which Pierre spoke of the dead man, from the careful, reverent tenderness with which Natasha spoke of him, the boy—just beginning to understand love—concluded that his father had loved Natasha and had, in dying, entrusted her to his friend. And that father whom the boy didn't remember became in his mind a divinity beyond human form, and he never thought of him without a swelling heart and tears of sorrow and exaltation. And so the boy was glad Pierre had come.
The guests welcomed Pierre because he always helped to enliven and unite any company he was in.
The adult members of the family, not to mention his wife, were pleased to have a friend back whose presence made life flow more smoothly and peacefully.
The old ladies were pleased with the presents he brought, and especially that Natasha would now be herself again.
Pierre sensed these different attitudes from the various worlds in the household and made haste to satisfy everyone's expectations.

Though he was the most absent-minded and forgetful of men, Pierre had managed—with the help of a list his wife had drawn up—to buy everything, not forgetting his mother-in-law's and brother-in-law's commissions, nor the dress material as a gift for Belova, nor toys for his nephews. In the early days of his marriage, this demand that he remember everything had struck him as strange, and he'd been impressed by the serious way Natasha insisted that he not forget a single item she'd entrusted to him, and by how offended she was when he returned from his first trip having forgotten everything. But in time he grew accustomed to it. Knowing that Natasha never asked him to buy anything for herself, and only gave him commissions for others when he offered, he now took an unexpected, childlike pleasure in buying presents for the whole household—never forgetting anything. If he deserved a scolding from Natasha, it was only for buying too many things and things that were too expensive. If he now incurred Natásha’s censure it was only for buying too many and too expensive things. To her other defects (as most people thought them, but which to Pierre were qualities) of untidiness and neglect of herself, she now added stinginess.

Since Pierre had begun living as a family man—a life that entailed heavy expenses—he had noticed to his surprise that he spent only half as much as before, and that his finances, which had lately been in disorder (mainly because of his first wife's debts), were beginning to improve.

Living was cheaper because it was regulated: the most expensive luxury of all—the kind of life that can change at any moment—was no longer his, nor did he want it. He felt that his way of life was now settled once and for all until death, and that to change it was not in his power; and so this way of life proved cheap.
With a cheerful, smiling face Pierre was sorting through his purchases.
"What do you think of this?" he said, unrolling a piece of fabric like a shopkeeper.
Natasha, who was sitting across from him with her eldest daughter on her lap, quickly turned her sparkling eyes from her husband to the things he was showing her.
"That's for Belova? Wonderful!" She felt the material. "I'll bet it was a ruble a yard?"
Pierre told her the price.

"Too much!" Natasha remarked. "The children and Mama will be so pleased though! Only you shouldn't have bought this for me," she added, unable to suppress a smile as she admired a gold comb set with pearls, the kind that was just coming into fashion.
"Adele kept tempting me—she kept telling me to buy it," Pierre said.
"When would I wear it?" And Natasha stuck it in her hair. "When I take little Masha into society? Maybe these will be back in style by then. Well—let's go now."
And gathering up the presents, they went first to the nursery and then to the old countess's rooms.
The countess was sitting with her companion Belova, playing patience as usual, when Pierre and Natasha came into the drawing room with packages in their arms.
The countess was now over sixty, completely gray, and wore a cap with a frill that framed her face. Her face had shriveled, her upper lip had sunk in, and her eyes were dim.

After the deaths of her son and husband in such quick succession, she felt like a being accidentally left behind in this world, forgotten and without any purpose or reason for existing. She ate, drank, slept or lay awake, but she did not live. Life gave her no impressions. She wanted nothing from life except peace, and that peace she could only find in death. But until death came, she had to go on living—that is, using her vital forces. What could be clearly observed in very young children—the need to exercise all their faculties—was visible in her too in the highest degree. She needed to eat, sleep, think, talk, cry, work, get angry, and so on, simply because she had a stomach, a brain, muscles, nerves, and a liver. She did all these things not because anything prompted her from outside, as people in the prime of life do—when the purpose behind the exercise of their faculties is hidden by the aim to which those faculties are directed. She talked only because she physically needed to exercise her tongue and lungs. She cried like a child because she needed to clear her nose, and so on.
So in the morning—especially if she'd eaten something rich the day before—she would feel a need to be angry, and she would pick the handiest target: Belova's deafness.
She would say something to her in a low voice from the other end of the room.
"It seems a little warmer today, my dear," she would murmur.
And when Belova replied: "Oh yes, they've come," she would mutter angrily: "Lord! How stupid and deaf she is!"

Another excuse would be her snuff, which was too dry, or too damp, or not ground fine enough. After these fits of irritation her face would turn yellow, and her maids knew by infallible signs when Belova would again be deaf, the snuff damp, and the countess's face yellow. Just as she needed to exercise her tongue, she sometimes needed to exercise her remaining capacity for thought—and the excuse for that was patience. When she needed to cry, the late count was the excuse. When she needed to feel anxious, Natasha's health was the excuse. When she needed to be sharp and angry, the excuse was Countess Mary. When she needed to exercise her voice—which usually happened around seven, after her after-dinner rest in a darkened room—the excuse was telling the same stories to the same audience over and over.

The old lady's condition was understood by the whole household, though no one ever spoke of it, and they all made every possible effort to satisfy her needs. Only by a rare glance exchanged with a sad smile between Nicholas, Pierre, Natasha, and Countess Mary did they reveal to each other their shared understanding of her state.

But those glances expressed something more: they said that she had played her part in life, that what they now saw was not her whole self, that we must all become like her, and that they were glad to give way to her, to restrain themselves for the sake of this once-dear creature who had been as full of life as they were now.
Only the truly heartless, the stupid members of that household, and the little children failed to understand this and avoided her.
